doc.title: Jamey Aebersold interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 26, 2022

title: Streaming project for the play-a-longs
summary: A streaming service with tempo, key and instrumentation controls and about 2,000 tracks.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: This has been fascinating, Mr. Aebersold. And I am privileged to talk to you and as I said kudos for what you’ve done. Do you have any other — you’re still doing it, and do you have any other specific projects that you’re contemplating?

We’re working on our streaming. We presently have our tracks but they can’t be played on Apple phones and so forth, and it’s a little cumbersome to use although we have quite a few people using it, all right? But we’re getting real close. As a matter of fact today was supposed to be the day that we were going to launch with about twelve friends of mine and have them work out the thing but I had a problem with it the other night. So it’s © Fillius Jazz Archive -20-

going to be easier to use, it will have tempo controls, and have access to about 2,000 tracks. They can have, if you’re playing “Now’s the Time” you can play it with piano, bass and drums, or piano and drums, or bass and drums. The only thing you can’t turn off is the drums. So they choose which instrumentation they want and then they can speed it up, slow it down, change the key. So I think this is going to bring in a much wider audience. Of the eight people that I’ve been working with at school only one has a CD player. Three of them I think listen to Spotify. The others don’t listen. That’s the impression I get. And of course they don’t listen to jazz. But after this class that we’re having every day I’ll bet some of them will start listening.
